title: Too Few Neurons, or Wrong Place

scenes.tts: Two children can both have a cerebral cortex that formed differently, for opposite reasons. In one child, the cortex is small, but its layers sit in the usual order. In the other, the cortex is thick and nearly smooth, and many neurons sit in the wrong place. Which step of building the cortex went wrong?
scenes.visual: two cortex slabs, one small with ordered rows, one thick with scattered neurons; a question appears
scenes.narration: Two children can both have a cerebral cortex that formed differently, for opposite reasons. In one child, the cortex is small, but its layers sit in the usual order. In the other, the cortex is thick and nearly smooth, and many neurons sit in the wrong place. Which step of building the cortex went wrong?

scenes.tts: Building a cortex is two jobs. First, radial glia line the fluid-filled ventricle. They divide to make more of themselves, and then to make neurons. Second, each new neuron moves outward along a radial glial fiber to its layer. So there are two broad ways to go wrong, and they can overlap. Too few neurons are made. Or neurons are made, but they stall on the way.
scenes.visual: tissue column: progenitors divide, a neuron climbs a fiber; two failure chips appear
scenes.narration: Building a cortex is two jobs. First, radial glia line the fluid-filled ventricle. They divide to make more of themselves, and then to make neurons. Second, each new neuron moves outward along a radial glial fiber to its layer. So there are two broad ways to go wrong, and they can overlap. Too few neurons are made. Or neurons are made, but they stall on the way.

scenes.tts: Take the first. Early on, progenitors divide in a symmetric way. Each division makes two progenitors, so each round doubles the pool. Later they switch to making neurons. In this simple model, a switch one round early halves the pool, and so halves the neurons. Primary microcephaly usually leaves the layers broadly normal. A leading idea says its genes act through this timing. Most of them, such as A S P M, encode proteins at the spindle pole of a dividing cell.

scenes.tts: A virus can strike the same step. Zika virus infected human cortical progenitors, grown from stem cells, far more readily than stem cells or immature neurons. It killed some progenitors and slowed the growth of the rest. Two cautions. This work used cultured cells and organoids, so it shows what the virus can do. And most infections in pregnancy do not produce microcephaly. Still, the virus attacks the cells that make neurons. So the cortex can be short of neurons, and tissue already built can be damaged too.
scenes.visual: three cell types; virus particles crowd the progenitor; fewer neurons result; two caution chips

scenes.tts: Now the second, lissencephaly. Here the progenitors were not the main problem. The neurons failed to travel. When L I S one was knocked down in rat embryos, progenitor divisions also stopped, and most new cells stayed many-branched. In the few that moved, neurons kept extending their leading process, but the nucleus barely moved. Another gene, D C X, makes doublecortin. It binds microtubules and stabilizes them in migrating neurons. A male has one X. If it carries the mutation, no neuron makes working doublecortin, and most neurons stall.

scenes.tts: A female has two X chromosomes. Early on, each cell silences one of them at random, so her cortex is a mosaic. On the standard interpretation, neurons with the normal X active reach the cortex. Neurons with the mutant X active stall partway and form a band. The usual reading is that each neuron follows the X it keeps active. So ask which step failed: too few neurons made, or neurons made but misplaced.
